Chapter 9





                                                                9-1

1. Describe the role of financial intermediaries
  such as commercial banks in the financial
  system
2. Discuss the three functions of money and
  how the money supply is measured
3. Analyze how the lending behavior of
   commercial banks affects the money supply
4. Explain how a central bank controls the
  money supply and how control of the money
   supply is related to inflation in the long run

                                                                       2

• The term "money" in economics has a
  specific meaning different from every day
  use
• To an economist:
  – Your paycheck is income
  – The income you don't spend is saving
  – The increase in the value of your stock is a
     capital gain
  – When your house appreciates, your wealth
     increases

                                                                       3

• A successful economy allocates its saving to the most
  productive investments
• The interest on deposits is one important reason
  people put their saving in banks
• The banking system improves the allocation of saving:
  – Provides information to savers about the possible
    uses of their funds
  – Help savers share the risks of individual
     investment projects
         • Risk sharing makes funding possible for projects that
         are risky but potentially very productive                                                                                                           9-4
                                                                         4

• Financial intermediaries are firms that
  extend credit to borrowers using funds raised
  from savers
  – Thousands of commercial banks accept deposits
    from individuals and businesses and make loans
  – Banks and other intermediaries specialize in
     evaluating the quality of borrowers
         • Principle of Comparative Advantage
         • Banks have a lower cost of evaluating opportunities
        than an individual would
         • Banks pool the saving of many individuals to make
         large loans
                                                                         5

• Banks gather information about potential
  investments
   – Evaluate the options
   – Direct saving
   – Service provided to depositors
• Banks provide access to credit for small
  businesses and homeowners
   – May be the only source of credit for some investments
• When banks make loans, they earn interest which,
   in turn, is paid to the bank's depositors

                                                                         6

• Having bank deposits makes payments easier
  – Checks
  – ATMs
  – Debit card
• Checks and debit cards are safer than cash
• Banks provide a record of your transactions
• The commercial banking system also plays a
  central role in determining the quantity of
 money in the economy
                                                                         7

• Money is any liquid asset that can be used in
  making purchases
   – Examples include coins and currency, checking
     account balances, and traveler's checks
   – Shares of stock are not money  not liquid
• Money has three principal uses
   1.Medium of exchange: Buyers give to sellers
    when they want to purchase goods and services
   2.Unit of account: Basic yardstick that people use
      to post prices, write contracts, record debts
   3.Store of value: People can use it to transfer
     purchasing power from the present to the future
                                                                            8

• Money makes barter unnecessary
  – Barter is trading goods directly
  – Barter requires a double coincidence of wants
         • Unlikely occurrence that two people each have a good
         the other wants
  – People would have to spend time searching for
     others to trade with – a huge waste of resources
  – This searching is unnecessary with money,
    an asset people readily accept

                                                                          9

• Commodity money:
   – Historically, money took the form of a
    commodity with intrinsic value
   – Examples: shells, copper, silver,
     gold, cigarettes in POW camps
• Fiat money:
   – Currently, money is without
      intrinsic value. Accepted as
    money because of the
    government
   – Example: paper money
                                                                           10

Why do merchants accept paper money in
exchange for valuable real goods?
•  Readily accepted by almost everyone as
  having value
• By law, it must be accepted as payment for
   all debts (Law of Legal Tender)
•  Only legal tender is acceptable for tax
  payments

                                                                             11

• Money is usually issued and controlled by the government
•  Private money can develop in certain circumstances
• An Ithaca Hour is worth $10, the average hourly wage of
  workers
   – 1,600 individuals have earned and spent this currency
          • Encourages local shopping
• LETS (Local Electronic Trading System) is electronic money
  from buying and selling goods and services
   – Used in UK, Australia, and New Zealand
•  Bitcoin virtual currency
   – Obtained through “mining” or in exchange for other currencies,
      products, and services
   – The price of Bitcoins is significantly volatile

                                                                         13

• The money supply (or money stock):
  the quantity of money available in the economy
• What assets should be considered part of the
  money supply? Here are some candidates:
   – Currency: the paper bills and coins in the hands of the
      (non-bank) public
   – Demand deposits: balances in bank accounts that
      depositors can access on demand for payments
      (by writing a
      check, using an
     ATM, or direct
     bank transfer)
                                                                        14

• M0 (most liquid measure): currency in
   circulation + commercial bank reserve
      “monetary base”
•  M1: M0 + demand deposits at
   commercial banks + other liquid
        deposits   “narrow money”
•  M2: M1 + savings accounts + time
   deposits (under $100,000) + retail
  money market funds

                                                                           15

• Republic of Gorgonzola begins with no
  banking system
  – Government issues 1 million guilders
  – Banks are created to store cash
         • Payments are made by withdrawing cash or
         writing checks
          – Checks tell bankers of change in ownership of the
              specified amount of guilders
  – Without interest, banks earn profits by
    charging depositors fees

                                                                       16

• All guilders (g) are deposited
         Assets                    Liabilities
   Currency  1,000,000 g   Deposits     1,000,000 g
• Bank reserves are cash or similar assets
  held by banks
  – Used to meet depositors' withdrawals and
    payments
  – Gorgonzola's banks have 100% reserves
         • 100% reserve banking is when banks' reserves equal
      100% of their deposits

                                                                         17

• Cash in a bank's vault (held as reserve) does not
  create extra money supply
   – Depositing a $100 bill in your checking account does not
     change the money supply
• Bank deposits available for use in transactions
  are part of the money supply
• Bankers realize that inflows and outflows from
  vaults leave some guilders unused
   – Only 10% of deposits are needed for transactions
   – 90% can be lent to borrowers for a fee -- interest

                                                                        18

• Currency held in the vault is the bank reserves
         Assets                    Liabilities
   Currency  100,000 g    Deposits     1,000,000 g
   Loans     900,000 g
• The reserve-deposit ratio is bank reserves
  divided by total deposits
• Fractional reserve banking system holds less
  bank reserves than deposits
   – The reserve-deposit ratio is less than 100%


                                                                         19

• Farmers borrow 900,000 guilders to buy supplies
   – Farmers spend the 900,000 guilders which are then
     deposited in the banks
         Assets                    Liabilities
   Currency  1,000,000 g   Deposits     1,900,000 g
   Loans     900,000 g
• Bank deposits are the entire money supply
   – Loan of 900,000 guilders increased the money supply
     by 900,000 guilders
• Banks are again holding excess reserves on
  deposits of 1,900,000 guilders
                                                                         20

• With deposits of 1,900,000 guilders and a
  reserve-deposit ratio of 10%, banks want only
  190,000 guilders in reserves
  – Currently holding 1,000,000 guilders
  – Loan 810,000 guilders
         Assets                    Liabilities
   Currency  1,000,000 g   Deposits     2,710,000 g
   Loans    1,710,000 g
  – Loan are spent and re-deposited
        • Excess reserves are created and re-loaned
                                                                         21

• Expansion of loans and deposits stops when
  reserves are 10% of deposits
   – 1,000,000 guilders available in each round as reserves
   – Deposits stabilize at 10,000,000 guilders

            Assets                          Liabilities
    Currency     1,000,000 g     Deposits        10,000,000 g
   Loans       9,000,000 g
• Beginning with 1,000,000 guilders in cash, the
  money supply is now 10,000,000 guilders
A fractional reserve banking system creates money,
but not wealth.
                                                                         22

• With 10% reserves, each guilder supports
  10 guilders in deposits
• Deposits in the banking system satisfy this
  relationship
    Bank reserves                 = Desired reserve-deposit ratio     Bank deposits
• Solving for bank deposits we get
                         Bank reserves    Bank deposits =                       Desired reserve-deposit ratio


                                                                         23

• Gorgonzola residents hold 500,000 guilders as
  currency
   – Deposit 500,000 guilders in the banks
   – Reserve-deposit ratio = 10%
   – Bank deposits = 500,000 / 0.10 = 5,000,000 guilders
   – Money supply = 500,000 cash + 5,000,000 deposits
     = 5,500,000 guilders

 Money supply = Currency held by public +
                          Bank reserves
                        Desired reserve-deposit ratio

                                                                          24

• Money multiplier: the amount of broad money
  generated with each dollar of reserves:
     Broad Money (M2) / Monetary Base (M0)
• At maximum, the money multiplier is
                 1/Reserve Ratio
• For example, $100 of reserves creates $1000 of
  money: Reserve Ratio = 0.10, money multiplier = 10
• The money multiplier is usually less than 1/Reserve
  Ratio as:
   – Some currency is held by the public not by banks
   – Banks also hold some excess reserves                                                                          25

Source: [link]

                                                                            26

• Suppose banks hold $500 billion in reserves and
  the public holds $500 billion in cash
   – Reserve-deposit ratio = 0.20
   – Money supply = $500 + (500 / 0.20) = $3,000
• As Christmas approaches, consumers reduce bank
  deposits by $100 billion
   – Banks have $400 billion in reserves; public holds $600
       billion cash
   – Money supply = $600 + ($400 / 0.20) = $2,600
• Reducing bank deposits reduces the money supply

                                                                         27

• An increase in the demand
   for physical money will
  reduce bank deposits
•  Reducing bank deposits
  reduces the money supply
   – Money supply tends to
      contract near festivals
   – Central banks usually
      increase money supply in
      preparation for seasonal
     events


                                                                          28

The money supply is 500 and currency held by the
public equals bank reserves. The desired reserve-
deposit ratio is 0.25. Find currency held by the public
and bank reserves.





                                                                         29

• A run on a bank:
  When people suspect that their bank is in trouble, they
  may “run” to the bank to withdraw their funds, holding
  currency instead of deposits
   – Under fractional-reserve banking, banks don’t have
    enough reserves to pay off ALL depositors, hence
     banks may be forced to close down
•  In response, banks may make fewer loans & hold more
  reserves to satisfy depositors
• These events increase cash holdings by the public,
  increase excess reserves, reverse the process of money
   creation, and cause money supply to shrink

                                                                         30

• During 1929-1933, a wave of bank runs and bank
  closings caused money supply to fall 28%
   – 11,000 banks (almost half of U.S. banks) failed
• Many economists believe this greatly contributed to the
   severity of the Great Depression
• Bank runs are less of a problem today because Central
  Banks stand behind commercial banks
•   If there is a problem, central banks lend as necessary to
  the commercial bank (they act as lender of last resort )
• Government agencies provide deposit insurance,
  discouraging depositors from participating in a bank run
  (PBoC in China, FDIC in US)
                                                                          31

• Japanese banks fell into severe trouble
  – Property values decreased and some loans on
     real estate went into default
  – Banks held stocks and the stock values
    decreased
• Japan had relied on banks to allocate its
  saving
  – Thin financial markets
  – Borrowers had difficulty obtaining credit
  – Small- and medium-sized businesses suffered
  – Credit shortages prolonged the recession as
    businesses struggled to fund new projects
                                                                         32

• Worst financial crisis since Great Depression, 1929
• Causes:
   – Housing market crash following the Subprime mortgage
       crisis
   – Financial deregulation, poorly understood derivatives,
     excessive risk taking
   – Globalization, rise of international shadow banking
   – Global imbalances: Excess savings in China, excess
     borrowing in the US
• Panic in financial markets, free fall of asset values
•  Credit crunch caused deep recession that followed

                                                                         33

• A financial crisis occurs when information
  flows in financial markets experience a
  particularly large disruption, with the result that
  financial frictions increase sharply and financial
  markets stop functioning. Then economic
   activity will collapse.
• Financial frictions: the asymmetric information
  that act as a barrier to efficient allocation of
  capital.


                                                                         34

Financial crises can begin in several ways:
• Mismanagement of financial
  innovation/liberalization
   – E.g. the 2008 global financial crisis
• Asset-Price Boom and Bust
• Increase in Uncertainty





                                                                        35

•  Tougher business conditions lead some financial institutions into
   insolvency, when net worth becomes negative.
•  Unable to pay off depositors or other creditors, some banks go
   out of business.
•   If severe enough, these factors can lead to a bank panic.
•  Uncertainty about the health of the banking system in general
  can lead to runs on banks, both good and bad, which will force
  banks to sell off assets quickly to raise the necessary funds.
•  With fewer banks operating, increasingly asymmetric information
  problem in financial markets deepen the financial crisis.
       declines in asset prices; firms lack funds for productive
investment; economic activity declines

                                                                         36

• The Fed is the central bank of the US
   – Created on December 23, 1913, after a series of
      financial panics (particularly the panic of 1907)
   – Responsible for monetary policy and the oversight
    and regulation of financial markets
• Monetary policy is deciding and managing the
  size of the nation's money supply
   – Money supply is controlled indirectly
          • Open-market purchase of government bonds from the
         pubic by the Fed increases bank reserves and the money
         supply
          • Open market sale of government bonds by the Fed to the
          public decreases reserves and money supply
                                                                         37

1. Open-Market Operations (OMOs): the purchase
and sale government bonds by the Central Bank.
• To increase money supply, CB buys gov. bonds or
  foreign currency, paying with new dollars.
     …which are deposited in banks, increasing
reserves
     …which banks use to make loans, increasing
money supply.
• To reduce money supply, CB sells gov. bonds or
  foreign currency, taking dollars out of circulation,
  reducing money supply.

                                                                        38

• An economy has 1,000 shekels in currency and
  bank reserves of 200 shekels
   – Reserve-deposit ratio = 0.2
   – Money supply = 1,000 + (200 / 0.2) = 2,000 shekels
• Central bank pays 100 shekels for a bond held by
  the public
   – Assume that all 100 shekels are deposited
   – Money supply = 1,000 + (300/ 0.2) = 2,500 shekels
   – 100 shekel increase in reserves leads to a 500
     shekel increase in the money supply

                                                                         39

2. Reserve Requirements (RR).
    Affect how much money banks can create by
   making loans.
• Central Banks rarely change the reserve
  requirements. Frequent changes would disrupt
  the banking system.
• To increase money supply, CB reduces RR.
   – Banks make more loans from each dollar of reserves,
     which increases money multiplier and money supply.
• To reduce money supply, CB raises RR, and the
  process works in reverse.

                                                                        40

3. The Discount Rate: the interest rate on loans the CB
makes to banks
• When banks are running low on reserves,
  they may borrow reserves from the CB.
• To increase money supply,
  Fed can lower discount rate, which encourages banks
  to borrow more reserves from CB.
  Banks are willing to make more loans, which increases
  the money supply.
• To reduce money supply, CB can raise discount rate.
  This discourages banks to borrow reserves and
  reduces loans and money supply.
                                                                           41

• On any day, banks with insufficient funds borrow
  from banks with excess funds
• The interest rate on these loans is called
   – in Hong Kong, the HIBOR
   – in Shanghai, the Shibor
   – in the US, the federal funds rate
• Because of HK’s linked exchange rate, HIBOR and the
  fed funds rate are highly correlated, so changes in the
  US fed funds rate have a big impact on HK’s economy
• The Fed uses OMOs to target the fed funds rate, so
  the Fed’s interest rate target & monetary policy are
  connected

• P = the price level
   (e.g., the CPI or GDP deflator)
• P  is the price of a basket of goods, measured
  in units of money
  – 1/P is the value of $1, measured in goods
• Example: basket contains one candy bar.
  – If P = $2, value of $1 is 1/2 candy bar
  – If P = $3, value of $1 is 1/3 candy bar
•  Inflation drives up prices, and drives down the
  value of money

                                                                         44

•  In the long run, the amount of money circulating
  and the level of prices are closely linked
   – Sustained high inflation rates occur with a comparably
     high growth rate of the money supply





                                                                        45

 money changes hands in transactions for
  final goods and services
                    Nominal GDP            Velocity =                  Money stock

• Nominal GDP is the price level (P) times
  real GDP (Y)

• The quantity equation states that money times
   velocity equals nominal GDP: M x V = P x Y
   – Restatement of the velocity definition
• Shows a relationship between money and price level
   – Suppose velocity and real GDP are constant
             V and Y, respectively
• The quantity equation becomes
           M x V = P x Y
   – An increase in the money supply by a given
     percentage would increase the price level by the
    same percentage
                                                                         50

M V = P Y
   % change in (M V) = % change in (P Y)
•  Percentage change in a product is the sum of
   the percentage changes in each variable
     % change in M + % change in V ≈
       % change in P + % change in Y
•  If the M grows 4% per year and V grows 1% per
  year, nominal GDP (P×Y) grows about 5% per year
   – If Y (real GDP) grows 3% per year, then percentage
    change in price is approximately 2% per year

                                                                            54

•  If real GDP is constant, then
   inflation rate = money growth rate
•  If real GDP is growing, then
   inflation rate < money growth rate
• The main takeaway:
  – Economic growth increases numbers of
     transactions
  – Some money growth is needed for these
     extra transactions
  – Excessive money growth causes inflation
                                                                         55

• Countries that have high inflation (>100% per
  year) are using inflation as a form of taxation
• When tax revenue is inadequate and ability to
  borrow is limited, govt may print money to pay
  for its spending.
• The revenue from printing money is the
  inflation tax: printing money causes inflation,
  which is like a tax on everyone who holds
  money.
• In the U.S., the inflation tax accounts for less
  than 3% of total revenue.
                                                                         56

• Monetary neutrality: the proposition that changes
   in the money supply do not affect real variables
• Doubling money supply causes all nominal prices to
  double; what happens to relative prices?
•  Initially, relative price of cd in terms of pizza is
     price of cd        $15/cd
               =          = 1.5 pizzas per cd
    price of pizza     $10/pizza
                             The relative price
•  After nominal prices double,                                                is unchanged.
                      $30/cd      price of cd               =          = 1.5 pizzas per cd
                      $20/pizza     price of pizza
                                                                          57

•  Similarly, when there is an increase in money
  supply and inflation, the real wage W/P remains
  unchanged
  – quantity of labor supplied does not change
  – quantity of labor demanded does not change
  – ratio of wages to prices remains unchanged
  – total employment of labor does not change
• The same applies to capital and other resources
• Since employment of all resources is unchanged,
   total output is also unchanged by money supply

                                                                          58

• The classical economists believed that monetary
  developments affect nominal variables, but not real
  variables
   –  If the central bank doubles the money supply, all nominal
      variables – including prices –
        will double
   – All real variables – including relative prices –
        will remain unchanged
   – Classical dichotomy: theoretical separation of nominal and
      real variables
• Modern economists believe money neutrality holds in
  the long run
• Money can have important real short-run effects
